passages.text: What causes fog to form, how it fades away and why it can linger for so long TOLEDO, Ohio (WTVG) - While fog is possible any time of year that conditions are right, there is a “fog season” here in NW Ohio and SE Michigan. It’s most common from October through March and sometimes into April, but fall fog has different mechanisms from the fog we usually get during the winter and early spring. There are many different types of fog, but during the autumn it’s typically radiation fog. For that you need clear skies because that’s what allows heat at the Earth’s surface to “radiate” out into space, hence the name. As temps at the surface drop close to the dewpoint, it helps to have a little moisture in the ground to saturate the air and facilitate fog formation. Lastly, very light or calm winds are needed because any gusts over 10 mph can quickly dissipate a bank of fog. This radiation fog usually forms during the overnight hours and early morning because that’s when conditions are right. However, it can start forming as early as the evening hours if temps rapidly drop to the dewpoint. Then, to get

Although gravity causes them to settle slowly, air currents and turbulence can keep them suspended. Over time, droplets may collide and merge, a process known as coalescence. Under suitable conditions, this can increase droplet size and contribute to the formation of drizzle. However, fog does not always produce precipitation, and most fog droplets remain small enough to stay airborne for considerable periods. Fog can also deposit moisture on surfaces. As droplets encounter leaves, grass, buildings, or other objects, they may collect there. In some environments, this deposition provides an additional source of water for vegetation and soils, especially when rainfall is limited. What determines how thick fog becomes? Fog thickness depends on the amount of moisture in the air, the strength and depth of cooling, and how air moves near the surface. A thin layer of fog may form when only a shallow layer of air reaches saturation. More extensive cooling or moisture supply can produce a deeper layer. passages.text: Fog is a cloud that forms at ground level when tiny water droplets, or sometimes ice crystals, become suspended in the air near Earth’s surface. It develops when air cools enough for water vapor to condense, or when moisture is added to the air until it becomes saturated. By scattering light, these tiny droplets reduce visibility and can make familiar landscapes, roads, and buildings difficult to see. Fog is a common weather phenomenon that can occur in nearly every part of the United States, from coastal regions and mountain valleys to agricultural plains and urban areas. Its formation depends on the interaction of temperature, humidity, wind, and the characteristics of the surrounding land or water. Different combinations of these factors produce several distinct types of fog, each with its own formation process and typical weather conditions. What causes fog to form? Air contains water vapor, the invisible gaseous form of water. The amount of water vapor air can hold before becoming saturated depends strongly on its temperature. Warm air can generally contain more water vapor than cold air before reaching saturation. When air cools, its capacity to hold water vapor decreases. Fog forecasting is hard because the phenomenon depends on small-scale processes, surface temperatures, soil moisture, local aerosol concentrations, wind variations over short distances, that weather models struggle to resolve. A radiation fog event might form over one field but not the one next to it. Sea fog might develop along a narrow coastal strip while the air just a few miles inland stays perfectly clear. Improving fog prediction remains one of the tougher challenges in operational meteorology. What Breathing Fog Actually Does to You People sometimes worry that breathing fog is harmful, and the answer depends almost entirely on what is dissolved in the droplets. Clean fog in a rural area is essentially a fine mist of nearly pure water. The droplets are large enough that most deposit in the nose and upper airways, and breathing them in is physiologically unremarkable. Acid fog is a different question. passages.text: [edit] The term fog is typically distinguished from the more generic term cloud in that fog is low-lying, and the moisture in the fog is often generated locally (such as from a nearby body of water, like a lake or ocean, or from nearby moist ground or marshes).[4] By definition, fog reduces visibility to less than 1 km (0.62 mi), whereas mist causes lesser impairment of visibility.[5][6] Formation [edit] Fog forms when the difference between air temperature and dew point is less than 2.5 °C (4.5 °F).[7][8] Fog begins to form when water vapor condenses into tiny water droplets that are suspended in the air. Some examples of ways that water vapor is condensed include wind convergence into areas of upward motion;[9] precipitation or virga falling from above;[10] daytime heating evaporating water from the surface of oceans, water bodies, or wet land;[11] transpiration from plants;[12] cool or dry air moving over warmer water;[13] and lifting air over mountains.[14] Water vapor normally begins to condense on condensation nuclei such as dust, ice, and salt in order to form clouds.[15][16] Fog, like its elevated cousin stratus, is a stable cloud deck which tends to form when a cool, stable air mass is

Many examples combine radiation cooling, cold-air drainage, and local moisture conditions. How fog droplets form and remain suspended Fog becomes visible when water vapor condenses into a large number of microscopic droplets. These droplets are generally much smaller than ordinary raindrops, allowing them to remain suspended in the air for extended periods. Condensation usually begins on tiny airborne particles. Water molecules collect on these particles, gradually forming droplets. The availability and properties of these particles can influence how many droplets form and how large they become. The droplets scatter light in different directions. When enough light is scattered away from its original path, objects appear faint, hazy, or invisible at a distance. The reduction in visibility depends on factors including droplet concentration, droplet size, and the distance light travels through the fog. Fog droplets do not simply fall to the ground as soon as they form. Their small size means air resistance strongly affects their movement. The temperature at which air becomes fully saturated is called the dew point, and when the air temperature drops to meet it, water vapor begins condensing into liquid droplets. If that condensation happens at ground level rather than up in the atmosphere, the result is fog rather than a cloud. In fact, fog and low clouds are physically the same phenomenon; the distinction is purely about altitude. The particles that fog droplets form around are called condensation nuclei, and they matter more than most people realize. Research in the Arctic has shown that highly hygroscopic (water-attracting) particles can trigger cloud and fog formation even when particle concentrations are extremely low, below ten particles per cubic centimeter, a threshold previously thought to be the minimum for any condensation to occur. In heavily polluted areas, the picture flips: a study of fog events in Paris found that local traffic and wood-burning emissions produced particles with low hygroscopicity, meaning the droplets that did form had to grow much larger before becoming fog droplets, with the critical wet diameter varying widely between fog events. The chemistry of whatever is floating in the air shapes what the fog looks like and how it behaves. Radiation Fog and the Clear-Night Setup The most common type of fog in many inland areas forms on clear, calm nights. After sunset, the ground radiates heat into the sky, and without clouds to reflect that heat back down, the surface cools rapidly. The thin layer of air just above the ground chills along with it. If that air is moist enough, it eventually reaches its dew point and fog begins to form. This is radiation fog, named for the radiative cooling that drives it. The recipe is specific: you need clear skies so there is nothing to trap outgoing heat, light winds so the cooling stays concentrated near the surface rather than getting mixed through a deep layer, and enough moisture in the air to reach saturation without extreme cooling. High-pressure weather systems are the classic setup because they bring stable, settled conditions with little cloud cover. Modeling work on radiation

This often causes freezing fog on mountaintops, where the cloud ceiling would not otherwise be low enough. Valley fog is a special case of radiation fog that forms in valleys. Pooling of cold air into valleys means fog can form more quickly and last longer, compared to over flat terrain. During winter, some valleys or basins will see fog lasting for several days in calm conditions.[34][35] In California's Central Valley, valley fog is often referred to as tule fog. Sea and coastal areas [edit] Sea fog (also known as haar or fret) is heavily influenced by the presence of sea spray and microscopic airborne salt crystals. Clouds of all types require minute hygroscopic particles upon which water vapor can condense. Over the ocean surface, the most common particles are salt from salt spray produced by breaking waves. Except in areas of storminess, the most common areas of breaking waves are located near coastlines, hence the greatest densities of airborne salt particles are there. Urban ice fog can become extremely dense and will persist day and night until the temperature rises. Upslope fog: When air rises along elevated terrain Upslope fog develops when moist air moves up a hillside, mountain slope, or elevated plateau. As the air rises, atmospheric pressure decreases, allowing the air to expand. Expansion causes the air to cool, even without direct heat loss to the surrounding ground. This cooling is called adiabatic cooling. If rising air cools to its dew point, water vapor condenses into droplets and fog forms along the terrain. Upslope fog is common where moist winds encounter elevated land. In the United States, it can develop along the eastern slopes of the Rocky Mountains and in other areas where moist air is forced upward by terrain. The process is closely related to cloud formation. When rising air becomes saturated, the resulting cloud may cling to a mountain slope or cover a ridge. Whether it is described as fog or a low cloud depends largely on its relationship to the ground and its effect on visibility. Upslope fog can cover extensive areas and last as long as moist air continues flowing toward and up the terrain. Unlike radiation fog, it does not depend on clear

passages.text: fog. This radiation fog usually forms during the overnight hours and early morning because that’s when conditions are right. However, it can start forming as early as the evening hours if temps rapidly drop to the dewpoint. Then, to get rid of the fog the following morning, the sun is the primary tool for the job. However, it doesn’t necessarily “burn the fog off”. Instead, it heats up the Earth’s surface, which causes the temperature to move farther from the dewpoint, thereby making conditions unsaturated and unfavorable for fog. Plus, that heating helps mix the atmosphere, which washes out that stagnant layer of air. But why does the fog last so much longer on some mornings compared to others? As the seasons progress and the sun gets lower in the sky, it takes longer to heat the Earth’s surface, which means the mixing process is slowed down. Plus, a thicker fog bank and any clouds overhead further delay that process, along with winds that just don’t pick up. In polluted urban areas, fog droplets can absorb sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and other pollutants, producing acidic solutions with pH values as low as 2 or 3, roughly as acidic as lemon juice. Controlled exposure studies have tested what this does to the lungs. In one experiment, asthmatic volunteers were exposed to sulfuric acid fogs at concentrations mimicking real Brussels fog (pH 2.5 and pH 3.5) for one hour at rest, and researchers found no significant changes in lung function or bronchial responsiveness. In a separate study that pushed harder, exposing both healthy and asthmatic subjects to sulfuric acid aerosols at concentrations up to 2,000 micrograms per cubic meter during heavy exercise, large fog-sized droplets (around 10 microns) still produced no marked lung function changes, though both groups reported increased respiratory symptoms in a dose-related pattern. The same study found that smaller droplets, around 0.9 microns, did cause measurable decreases in lung function among asthmatics at the highest concentrations. The practical takeaway is that typical outdoor fog, even moderately polluted fog, does not appear to cause acute lung function problems in most people during short exposures. passages.text: Fog forms when air cools to the point where its moisture condenses into tiny suspended water droplets, typically around microscopic airborne particles like dust, soot, or sea salt. The World Meteorological Organization defines it as a suspension of very small water droplets in the air that reduces visibility at Earth’s surface, and those droplets range from a few tenths of a micron to a few tens of microns across. But the cooling can happen in several different ways, which is why fog shows up in such different settings: over cold ocean water, in river valleys after sunset, on mountain slopes, and even in arid deserts on the right night. The details of how the air loses heat, and what particles are floating in it, determine whether fog forms at all and how long it lasts. The Two Ingredients Every Fog Needs Strip away the complexity and fog requires just two things: air that has cooled enough to become saturated with moisture, and particles for that moisture to condense onto. Except in areas of storminess, the most common areas of breaking waves are located near coastlines, hence the greatest densities of airborne salt particles are there. Condensation on salt particles has been observed to occur at humidities as low as 70%, thus fog can occur even in relatively dry air in suitable locations such as the California coast. Typically, such lower humidity fog is preceded by a transparent mistiness along the coastline as condensation competes with evaporation, a phenomenon that is typically noticeable by beachgoers in the afternoon. Another recently discovered source of condensation nuclei for coastal fog is kelp seaweed. Researchers have found that under stress (intense sunlight, strong evaporation, etc.), kelp releases particles of iodine which in turn become nuclei for condensation of water vapor, causing fog that diffuses direct sunlight.[36] Sea smoke, also called steam fog or evaporation fog, is created by cold air passing over warmer water or moist land.[37] It may cause freezing fog or sometimes hoar frost. At 100% relative humidity, the air cannot hold additional moisture, thus the air will become supersaturated if additional moisture is added. Fog commonly produces precipitation in the form of drizzle or very light snow. Drizzle occurs when the humidity attains 100% and the minute cloud droplets begin to coalesce into larger droplets.[19] This can occur when the fog layer is lifted and cooled sufficiently, or when it is forcibly compressed from above by descending air. Drizzle becomes freezing drizzle when the temperature at the surface drops below the freezing point.
